questions.q: What kind of business process is an accumulating snapshot fact table built for?
options: A pipeline with a defined start, a predictable sequence of stages, and an end, like an order moving through fulfillment
A single instantaneous event, like one click on a webpage
A value that needs to be captured on a fixed schedule regardless of activity
A table that never needs any dimension keys
questions.explain: Microsoft's guidance describes accumulating snapshot fact tables as tracking a process's progress through distinct milestones over a well-defined period, unlike a single-event transaction fact.

questions.q: In the f_OrderFulfillment example, what happens to a milestone's date key before that milestone occurs?
options: It holds a special "N/A" member instead of a real date, since you can't reference an event that hasn't happened yet
The entire row is deleted until every milestone happens
It is left as SQL Server NULL, which is always allowed for dimension keys
The row is duplicated once for every possible future milestone
questions.explain: Dimension keys are kept NOT NULL by using a special dimension member to represent an unreached milestone, rather than a literal date that doesn't yet exist.

questions.q: Why does f_OrderFulfillment reference the Date dimension four separate times (OrderDate, PickDate, ShipDate, DeliverDate)?
options: Because it's a role-playing dimension — the same physical Date dimension used in multiple distinct roles on one fact table
Because SQL Server requires a new copy of a dimension table for every foreign key
Because each milestone actually needs a differently structured date table
It's a modeling mistake and should reference only one date key
questions.explain: One physical dimension, referenced multiple times for distinct purposes on the same fact table, is exactly what a role-playing dimension is — covered fully in Chapter 3.

questions.q: Why isn't the accumulating snapshot fact table's ETL pattern insert-only, unlike a transaction fact table?
options: The load has to find the existing row for a process instance and UPDATE it every time a new milestone is reached, until the process completes
Accumulating snapshot tables never get new rows inserted at all
SQL Server automatically updates fact tables without any ETL logic
It uses exactly the same load pattern as a transaction fact table
questions.explain: One row tracks a process instance across its whole lifecycle, so the load must locate and update that row as each milestone occurs — a fundamentally different pattern than insert-only.

questions.q: Why are the measures in f_OrderFulfillment durations (like DaysToShipAfterPick) rather than dollar amounts?
options: Because the real operational question this fact table answers is how long the process spent at each stage, not a monetary total
Dollar amounts are never allowed in any fact table
Durations are the only data type SQL Server permits in a fact table
Because accumulating snapshot tables can't have more than one measure
questions.explain: Durations between milestones are what an accumulating snapshot is designed to surface — insight into how a workflow performs stage by stage.
